meta.title: Who really said "He may be a son of a bitch, but he's our son of a bitch"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not FDR: Time first pinned it on him in 1948, after his death, as Washington gossip. The quip is anonymous political folklore in print since 1868.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'He may be a son of a bitch, but he's our son of a bitch'?
meta.ogDescription: No record shows Roosevelt said it. The first FDR credit is a 1948 Time rumor; the 'he's our rascal' formula goes back to an anonymous 1868 editorial.

answer.label: Not Franklin D. Roosevelt — an anonymous political quip
answer.authorDates: American political folk saying · earliest match known to Quote Investigator: 1868
answer.sourceLine: No speech, letter or press conference shows Roosevelt saying it. The first time it is pinned on him is a 1948 Time article, published after his death, which passes it on as “a story told around Washington.” Quote Investigator ↗ traces the “he’s our rascal” formula back to an anonymous 1868 newspaper editorial.

source.heading: Where the Roosevelt version comes from

docMeta.dd: Secondhand: “a story told around Washington” after Roosevelt’s death (he died in 1945)
The Daily Journal, Wilmington, N.C., July 26, 1868: “Ah! but he is our rascal” (per Quote Investigator)

source.excerpt: To prime President Roosevelt for the visit, Sumner Welles sent him a long solemn memorandum about Somoza and Nicaragua. According to a story told around Washington, Roosevelt read the memo right through, wisecracked: “As a Nicaraguan might say, he’s a sonofabitch but he’s ours.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ (2021): the earliest match known to QI is an anonymous 1868 Wilmington, N.C., editorial (“Ah! but he is our rascal”). QI concludes that the evidence for Roosevelt is weak and that “the first attribution to F.D.R was based on a posthumous rumor.”
Time, Nov. 15, 1948 ↗: the first Roosevelt version, introduced with “According to a story told around Washington.”

Wikiquote ↗ lists the line as Disputed. It reports that FDR Library archivist Donald Schewe searched Roosevelt’s papers and found no evidence, and that he judged it “was not the kind of language that Roosevelt used” (citing Robert A. Pastor, Condemned to Repetition, 1987).
Fred Shapiro, Yale Book of Quotations editor ↗ (2011): the 1948 Time story is “the earliest version I know of” of the Roosevelt attribution.
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest attribution to Roosevelt that Quote Investigator and Fred Shapiro cite. The wording is not the popular one (“he’s a sonofabitch but he’s ours”), and Time reports it as hearsay, not as something it witnessed or documented.

author.name: Anonymous
author.heading: Who actually coined it
author.metaLine: Anonymous · U.S. political folk saying, in print since 1868
author.bio: Nobody can be named. The earliest version Quote Investigator has found is an unsigned 1868 editorial in Wilmington, North Carolina. In it, two unnamed politicians argue about a shady candidate: “He is a great rascal.” “Ah! but he is our rascal.” Over the next century the insult changed (scalawag, scoundrel, so-and-so, son-of-a-bitch, bastard, dictator), and the line was credited to one famous figure after another, from Thaddeus Stevens and Abraham Lincoln to Franklin Roosevelt, Cordell Hull and Lyndon Johnson.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest attribution to Roosevelt: “Nicaragua: I’m the Champ,” Time, November 15, 1948, reported as “a story told around Washington.” Earliest version of the formula known to Quote Investigator: “Our Rebels,” The Daily Journal (Wilmington, NC), July 26, 1868, 2. See Garson O’Toole, Quote Investigator, February 24, 2021, https://quoteinvestigator.com/2021/02/24/rascal/.

misattribution.heading: One quip, many owners
misattribution.intro: The “he’s our ___” formula has been handed from one famous name to another for more than 150 years. Even the Roosevelt version disagrees with itself about who he was supposedly talking about.

items.why: First credited to him in 1948, after his death, as Washington hearsay in Time ↗. An FDR Library archivist found no record of it (Wikiquote ↗).

In 1968 Alistair Cooke said Roosevelt was talking about a Democratic big-city mayor. In 1969 the Seattle paper Helix said it was Rafael Trujillo of the Dominican Republic (Quote Investigator ↗). Dick Morris later tied it to Franco (Washington Monthly ↗).
In 1979 Christopher Hitchens wrote that Hull “coined” the line about Somoza (Quote Investigator ↗). Michael Wood credited Hull with saying it about Trujillo (Washington Monthly ↗).
Credited with “He may be a dictator, but at least he’s our dictator” in a 1990 citation (Quote Investigator ↗).

items.who: Thaddeus Stevens, Benjamin Butler, Abraham Lincoln
items.why: Stevens got the credit by 1875, Butler by 1877, and Lincoln (who died in 1865) in an 1889 anecdote, all after the anonymous 1868 version (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: it is an anonymous political saying that has been evolving since at least 1868. In Quote Investigator’s ↗ words, the evidence for Roosevelt “was weak,” and his attribution rests on a posthumous rumor.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Roosevelt
lead: The line spells out a hard-nosed bargain in Cold War foreign policy: putting up with a brutal ally because he is on your side. Pinning it on FDR and Somoza gave that idea a famous speaker and a famous dictator. But Quote Investigator ↗ shows the joke was old long before Roosevelt. It began as party-loyalty humor about crooked candidates, and in 1934 John Franklin Carter’s book The New Dealers told it about two unnamed politicians: “Blank isn’t so bad. He’s our son-of-a-bitch!”

The exact popular wording turns up in Quote Investigator’s chronology in 1962, in Charles Einstein’s baseball book A Flag for San Francisco. There, San Francisco redevelopment official M. Justin Herman used it about a stadium, Candlestick Park: “He may be a son of a bitch, but he’s our son of a bitch.”
context.detailsSummary: Was any of this ever documented?
detailsBody: As Kevin Drum ↗ put it in 2006, after comparing the competing versions: “we don’t know who said it, who it was said of, or where it came from.”
